description: New to AI assistants, or frustrated by generic answers? This free, beginner-friendly course teaches the skill behind every great AI result: explaining a task clearly. You will learn how today's assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot respond to your words, the five building blocks of a good prompt (Task, Context, Audience, Format, Examples), and how to be specific without writing essays. You will practise iterating, controlling formats, and using the features that matter in 2026: thinking modes for harder problems, projects and custom instructions that remember your context, web search and deep research with sources you can check, and prompting with files, photos, screenshots, voice and image generators. A library of more than fifty ready-to-adapt patterns covers writing, analysis, brainstorming, learning and planning. Finally, you will learn a simple routine for checking AI work and protecting private information. No technical background needed.

lessons.title: How AI assistants respond to your words
lessons.body:
### Welcome

If you have ever typed a question into an AI assistant and received an answer that was vague, generic or slightly off, this course is for you. You do not need any technical background. By the end, you will have a simple method you can use for almost any task, plus a library of more than fifty ready-to-use prompt patterns.

A **prompt** is simply what you give the AI: your question, your instructions, any text you paste in, and any examples. Prompt engineering sounds technical, but at its heart it is the skill of *explaining a task clearly*, the same skill that makes someone a good manager, teacher or client.

### A simple picture of how it works

AI chat assistants are built on large language models. You do not need the maths, but one idea helps a lot:

**The model writes the response that seems most likely to fit what you gave it.**

It has learned patterns from an enormous amount of text: how emails are written, how recipes are structured, how explanations flow. When you give it a short, vague request, it fills the gaps with the most typical, average answer. When you give it a clear, specific request, it can produce something tailored to you.

That is why these two prompts give very different results:

```text
Write a post about our bakery.
```

```text
Write a friendly Instagram caption (under 60 words) announcing that our
family bakery in Lahore now opens at 7am on weekdays, so office workers
can grab fresh parathas and chai before work. Include one emoji and a
call to action to visit.
```

The first gets a generic bakery post. The second gets something you could actually publish.

### Three things to know from day one

**1. It does not know your situation unless you tell it.** The AI does not know your business, your audience, your deadline or your preferences. Anything important must be in the prompt.

**2. It can be confidently wrong.** AI assistants sometimes state things that sound right but are not, including made-up facts, figures, quotes or sources. This is often called a "hallucination". Always check facts that matter, especially numbers, dates, names, legal, medical or financial information.

**3. It is a conversation.** You can reply, correct and refine. Your first prompt is a starting point, not a final exam. Some of the best results come from the second or third message.

### What AI assistants are good at

- Drafting: emails, posts, outlines, summaries, first versions of almost anything.
- Rewriting: changing tone, length, reading level or language.
- Explaining: breaking down a topic you do not understand, at your level.
- Brainstorming: generating many options quickly.
- Organising: turning messy notes into structured lists, tables or plans.

### Where to be careful

- Up-to-date facts: depending on the tool, it may not know recent events unless it can search the web. Check the tool's settings or ask it whether it is using live search.
- Precise calculations on large data: helpful, but verify.
- Personal or confidential information: think before pasting customer data, passwords or private documents. Check your organisation's rules and the tool's privacy settings.
- Important decisions: use AI to think, draft and compare, but you make the call.

### A tiny experiment to try now

Open any AI assistant you have access to and try this pair:

```text
Give me tips for a job interview.
```

Then:

```text
I have a video interview on Thursday for a junior marketing role at a
skincare brand. I'm nervous about the question "Tell me about yourself".
Give me a 60-second answer structure and a sample answer I can adapt,
based on this background: 1 year running social media for a family
restaurant, grew followers from 800 to 3,000.
```

Notice how much more useful the second answer is. You did not need special words or tricks. You just gave the AI what a helpful friend would need to know.

### What you will learn in this course

- The anatomy of a good prompt (module 1)
- How to be clear and specific, and how to give context and examples (module 2)
- How to iterate and control the format of answers (module 3)
- Using modern assistant features well: thinking modes, projects and memory, web research, files, photos, voice and image generation (module 4)
- A practical library of prompt patterns for writing, analysis, brainstorming, learning and planning (module 5)
- The everyday mistakes that hold people back, and how to check AI work (module 6)

Take your time, try every example, and keep a note of the prompts that work for you. By the end, you will have your own personal prompt toolkit.

### What changed in the latest assistants

The assistants you will use in 2026 (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and others) do much more than answer typed questions. Most of them can now:

- **Think before answering.** Many offer a "thinking" or "reasoning" mode that spends extra time working through harder problems. It is slower, but often better for maths, planning and tricky decisions. You will learn when to use it in module 4.
- **Search the web** and show the sources they used, so you can check them.
- **Read files and images:** PDFs, spreadsheets, photos of whiteboards, screenshots of error messages.
- **Listen and speak** in voice mode.
- **Remember context** through features such as projects, custom instructions or memory, so you do not repeat yourself every time.
- **Create images** from a description.

The core skill is the same across all of these: explain what you want clearly. A vague request to a powerful assistant still gets a generic answer.

### A mental model worth keeping: the smart new colleague

Picture a brilliant new colleague on their first day. They are fast, well read and eager, but they know nothing about your business, your customers or your taste, and they will not ask questions unless you invite them to. Everything in this course is about briefing that colleague well. When an answer disappoints, ask yourself: "What would a smart new colleague have needed to know?" The fix is almost always there.

### Hands-on: your first three experiments

Open any assistant and run these three short experiments. Keep a note of what you notice.

**Experiment 1: vague versus specific.**

```text
Give me ideas for a weekend.
```

```text
Give me 5 ideas for a relaxed Saturday in Dubai for a family with two
children aged 6 and 9, budget under 400 AED, mostly indoors because of
the heat. One line each, with a rough cost.
```

**Experiment 2: ask it what it needs.**

```text
I want to write a short thank-you message to a teacher who helped my son
this year. Before writing anything, ask me 3 questions so you can make
it personal.
```

**Experiment 3: test its honesty.**

```text
What were the three biggest news stories this morning?
```

If your assistant is not searching the web, a good answer admits it cannot know today's news. If it lists stories without sources, treat them as unreliable. This one test teaches you more about the tool than any feature list.

### How to know it is working

After this lesson you should notice two things: your prompts naturally include who, what and why, and you catch yourself checking any fact that matters. Those two habits already put you ahead of most users.

lessons.title: The anatomy of a good prompt
lessons.body:
### Five building blocks

Most great prompts contain some or all of five building blocks. You will not need every block every time, but knowing them means you will never be stuck.

1. **Task:** what you want done. Start with a clear action verb: write, summarise, explain, compare, list, rewrite, plan.
2. **Context:** the background the AI needs: who you are, the situation, the goal.
3. **Audience:** who the result is for, and what they already know.
4. **Format:** what the output should look like: length, structure, tone, language.
5. **Examples or constraints:** a sample of what good looks like, and any rules (what to include, what to avoid).

A handy memory aid: **Task, Context, Audience, Format, Examples** (T-CAFE).

### Building a prompt, block by block

Let's build a prompt for a common task: asking a landlord to fix a broken heater.

**Task only:**

```text
Write an email to my landlord.
```

**Add context:**

```text
Write an email to my landlord asking them to fix the heater in my flat.
It stopped working 5 days ago and I reported it by phone on Monday
but nobody has come.
```

**Add audience:**

```text
... My landlord is polite but slow to respond, and I want to keep a good
relationship.
```

**Add format:**

```text
... Keep it under 150 words, polite but firm, with a clear request for a
repair date by Friday. Include a subject line.
```

**Add constraints:**

```text
... Don't threaten legal action. Mention that I have a young child at home.
```

The final prompt is five or six sentences long, and the email it produces will need only minor edits. The first version would have needed a full rewrite.

### Why each block matters

- **Without a clear task,** the AI may explain instead of write, or write instead of list.
- **Without context,** it invents a generic situation.
- **Without audience,** it guesses the level of detail and tone. An explanation for a ten-year-old and one for a finance director are very different.
- **Without format,** you get whatever length and structure is typical, often too long.
- **Without examples or constraints,** it cannot match your style or avoid things you dislike.

### Order and layout

For short prompts, natural sentences work well. For longer prompts, especially when you paste in text, it helps to separate the parts clearly:

```text
TASK: Summarise the customer feedback below for my manager.

CONTEXT: We are a small online clothing shop. This is feedback from
our last 30 orders.

AUDIENCE: My manager, who has 2 minutes to read it.

FORMAT: 3 bullet points of main themes, then 1 suggested action.

FEEDBACK:
---
(paste feedback here)
---
```

Putting pasted text inside quotation marks or clear markers helps the AI tell your instructions apart from the material you want it to work on.

### Role: an optional sixth block

You may see advice to start with "You are a..." ("You are an experienced career coach"). A role can help set the tone and level of expertise, especially in combination with the other blocks. But a role alone is not magic; "You are a world-class marketer. Write a post." still lacks context, audience and format. Think of role as seasoning, not the meal.

### A worked example from start to finish

A shop owner in Dubai wants to reply to a customer review.

```text
TASK: Write a reply to the Google review below.
CONTEXT: I own a small phone repair shop in Dubai. The customer waited
2 hours because a part was delayed. We gave a 10% discount.
AUDIENCE: The customer, but also future customers reading the reviews.
FORMAT: Under 80 words, warm and professional, in English.
CONSTRAINTS: Apologise sincerely, don't make excuses, invite them back.

REVIEW:
"Repair was good but I waited 2 hours with no updates. Not happy."
```

The result will be specific (it mentions the wait and the missing updates), appropriately short and on-tone.

### Quick self-check before you press enter

Ask yourself:

- Would a smart stranger understand what I want?
- Did I say who it is for?
- Did I say how long and in what format?
- Is there anything I would be annoyed to see? If so, say so.

This takes ten seconds and saves many rounds of back-and-forth.

### Hands-on: build a T-CAFE prompt in five minutes

Pick a real task from this week. Fill in this template, deleting any line you do not need:

```text
TASK: [action verb + what you want, e.g. "Write a WhatsApp message..."]
CONTEXT: [who you are, the situation, the goal]
AUDIENCE: [who will read it and what they care about]
FORMAT: [length, structure, tone, language]
EXAMPLES / CONSTRAINTS: [a sample you like; things to include or avoid]
```

Here is a filled-in version from a freelance photographer in Karachi:

```text
TASK: Write a WhatsApp message confirming a wedding shoot booking.
CONTEXT: I am a freelance photographer. The couple paid a 30% deposit
yesterday. The shoot is on the mehndi and baraat days.
AUDIENCE: The bride's elder sister, who is organising everything and is
very busy.
FORMAT: Under 70 words, warm and professional, English with one Urdu
greeting. Use line breaks, no bullet points.
CONSTRAINTS: Mention that the balance is due one week before the first
event. Do not mention prices.
```

### The same structure works in every assistant

T-CAFE is not tied to one product. It works in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot or any assistant built into your email, documents or phone. If your assistant supports **custom instructions** or **projects** (see module 4), you can store the parts that never change, such as who you are and your preferred style, so each new prompt only needs the task and the details.

### Common beginner questions

**Do I need to write labels like TASK and CONTEXT?** No. They help you remember the parts and help the AI separate them, especially when you paste material. Natural sentences work fine for short prompts.

**How long should a prompt be?** As long as it needs to be. Two sentences for a quick rewrite; half a page when you paste material and have specific requirements. Length is not the goal; missing information is the enemy.

**Should I be polite?** Politeness does no harm and keeps your habits pleasant, but clarity matters far more than "please" and "thank you".

### How to know your prompt is good

Run the stranger test: hide the AI's answer and show only your prompt to a friend. If they could do the task without asking you a single question, your prompt is ready. If they ask "Who is this for?" or "How long?", add that information.

modules.title: Clarity, context and examples
modules.summary: Learn to be specific without writing essays, give the background that matters, and use examples to show exactly what you want.

lessons.title: Clarity and specificity
lessons.body:
### Vague words are the enemy

Words like "good", "short", "professional", "engaging" and "detailed" mean different things to different people. The AI has to guess what you mean, and it guesses average. Clarity means replacing vague words with concrete ones.

| Vague | Specific |
|---|---|
| Make it short | Under 100 words |
| Make it professional | Formal, no slang, suitable for a bank's client email |
| Make it engaging | Start with a question; use one short personal example |
| Explain it simply | Explain for a 12-year-old using an everyday comparison |
| Give me some ideas | Give me 10 ideas, each in one sentence |

### Say what you want, not only what you don't

"Don't be boring" gives the AI nothing to aim at. "Use a surprising fact in the first sentence and keep sentences under 20 words" does. It is fine to include things to avoid, but pair each "don't" with a "do".

### Be specific about the goal

The same task changes with the goal. Compare:

- "Write a LinkedIn post about our new product."
- "Write a LinkedIn post about our new product *to get small-business owners to book a free demo*."

The second tells the AI what the post is *for*, so it can choose a call to action, the right benefits and a suitable tone.

### Quantities and limits

Numbers are one of the easiest ways to be specific:

- How many? ("5 subject lines")
- How long? ("2 paragraphs", "under 50 words", "a 3-minute speech")
- How detailed? ("one sentence per point")
- By when? ("a plan for the next 4 weeks")

Word counts are approximate for AI, so give a range ("80 to 120 words") and check.

### One task at a time (or clearly listed)

Mixing several requests in one long paragraph invites the AI to do some and skip others. Either ask one thing at a time, or number the requests:

```text
Please do three things with the notes below:
1. Summarise them in 5 bullet points.
2. List any decisions we made, with the owner's name.
3. Draft a short follow-up email to the team.
```

### Worked example: from vague to clear

A teacher in Manchester wants help with a parents' newsletter.

Vague:

```text
Help me with a newsletter.
```

Clear:

```text
Write the opening section (about 120 words) of our Year 4 class
newsletter for parents. Topics: the school trip to the science museum
on 14 March (permission slips due 7 March) and our new reading challenge.
Tone: warm and upbeat, easy to read on a phone. End with a reminder to
return slips.
```

Everything the AI needs is there: section, length, audience, topics, dates, tone and ending.

### Clarity is not length

Being specific does not mean writing an essay. A clear 40-word prompt beats a rambling 300-word one. Aim for every sentence to add information the AI could not guess. If a sentence does not change the result, cut it.

### A useful trick: let the AI ask you

When you are not sure what details matter, ask the AI to interview you first:

```text
I want to write a speech for my sister's wedding. Before you write
anything, ask me up to 5 questions about what you need to know.
```

This is one of the most powerful beginner techniques. The AI's questions show you which details matter, and the final result will be far more personal.

### Common clarity mistakes

- Using pronouns without context ("rewrite it", when "it" is not in the chat).
- Assuming the AI knows internal names ("update the Q3 deck" means nothing to it).
- Leaving out the most important constraint ("it must fit on one slide").
- Changing your mind halfway through a long prompt without editing earlier parts.

### Summary checklist

- Replace vague adjectives with concrete descriptions or numbers.
- State the goal, not only the task.
- Number multiple requests.
- Pair every "don't" with a "do".
- When unsure, ask the AI to ask you questions first.

### Hands-on: the vague-word hunt

Take any prompt you wrote recently and underline every word that a stranger could interpret in two ways. Then replace each one using this checklist:

```text
Vague word        Ask yourself                      Replace with
"short"           How short, measured how?          "under 80 words" / "3 bullets"
"professional"    Professional for whom?            "formal, for a bank's client email"
"catchy"          What makes it catch attention?    "start with a question or number"
"simple"          Simple for which reader?          "for a 12-year-old" / "no jargon"
"soon"            By when?                          "by Thursday 5pm"
"some ideas"      How many, how detailed?           "8 ideas, one line each"
```

Now try the improved prompt and compare the two answers side by side. Most people are surprised by how much a few concrete words change the result.

### Worked example: a small business owner in Jeddah

Before:

```text
Write something for our new menu.
```

After:

```text
Write a 3-line description for each of these 4 new dishes on our café's
Instagram story. Audience: university students in Jeddah. Tone: playful,
modern. Each description: dish name, one sensory detail, price in SAR.
Dishes: saffron latte (18), date cheesecake (22), halloumi wrap (25),
mango sparkling tea (15).
```

The second prompt fixes the destination (Instagram story), the audience, the tone, the structure and supplies the real facts, so nothing needs to be invented.

### Specific, not rigid

Being specific does not mean controlling every word. Leave the AI room where you want creativity ("suggest the angle") and be exact where you have firm requirements ("price in SAR, under 30 words"). A useful habit is to separate **must-haves** from **nice-to-haves**:

```text
Must: under 100 words, mention the 14 March deadline, friendly tone.
Nice to have: a light joke, a question at the end.
```

### How to measure your progress

Over the next week, count how many follow-up messages you need before an answer is usable. When your prompts are clear, that number drops from three or four to one or zero. That is the most practical measure of clarity you have.

lessons.title: Giving context and examples
lessons.body:
### Context: what a helpful colleague would need to know

Imagine asking a colleague to "draft a reply to this client". A good colleague would ask: Who is the client? What happened? What do we want to happen next? Is there anything sensitive? The AI needs the same information, but it cannot ask unless you invite it to. Giving context up front is the single biggest upgrade most people can make.

Useful context usually covers:

- **Who you are:** "I run a two-person wedding photography business."
- **The situation:** "A couple is asking for a discount because their budget changed."
- **The goal:** "I want to keep the booking without cutting my price by more than 10%."
- **Constraints:** "We have already paid for their venue permit."
- **Relevant material:** the email thread, your price list, your policy.

### How much context is enough?

Enough that the AI does not have to invent anything important. Not so much that the key point is buried. A good rule: include anything that would change the answer. Your company's founding year probably does not; your refund policy probably does.

### Pasting material in

Often the best context is the actual document: the email you are replying to, your notes, a product description. Paste it in and label it clearly:

```text
Here is the client's email:
---
(paste here)
---

Here is our package price list:
---
(paste here)
---

Draft a reply that offers the smaller package as an alternative.
```

Before pasting, remove anything private you would not want to share, such as personal phone numbers, ID numbers, passwords or confidential figures, and follow your workplace rules about AI tools.

### Examples: show, don't just tell

Sometimes describing what you want is hard, but showing it is easy. An example of the style, format or tone you like is often worth a paragraph of instructions.

**Example of tone:**

```text
Write 3 more product descriptions in the same style as this one:

"Soft as a Sunday morning. Our cotton hoodie is pre-washed, so it feels
broken-in from day one. Oversized fit. Machine-washable. Made to be lived in."

Products: linen shirt, wool beanie, canvas tote bag.
```

The AI picks up the short sentences, the sensory opening and the rhythm.

**Example of format:**

```text
Turn my notes into this format:
Name - Role - One key point they made

Example:
Sara - Designer - Wants fewer colours on the homepage
```

### Tips for good examples

- **Use one to three examples.** For most everyday tasks, that is plenty.
- **Vary them** if you want variety in the output. If all your examples are about coffee, the AI may drift toward coffee.
- **Say what to copy.** "Copy the tone and length, not the content."
- **Use real examples you like,** such as a past email that worked well or a post that performed well.

### Worked example: a job application

Without context:

```text
Write a cover letter for a data analyst job.
```

With context and an example:

```text
Write a cover letter for a junior data analyst role at a healthcare
charity in Birmingham.

About me: recent maths graduate, built an Excel dashboard tracking
volunteer hours for my university society, basic SQL.

What they want (from the job ad):
---
(paste the key requirements)
---

Style: confident but humble, short paragraphs, under 300 words.
Here is an opening line I like the style of:
"Numbers only matter when they help people make better decisions."
Don't reuse that line; match its directness.
```

This letter will mention the real dashboard, match the job's requirements and sound like a person, not a template.

### When the AI gets something wrong, add context

If the answer misses the mark, the fix is often more context, not different wording. Ask yourself: what did the AI not know that it needed to? Then add it: "Note: our customers are mostly retired people, so avoid slang."

### Summary

- Context answers who, what, why and what matters.
- Paste real material, clearly labelled and cleaned of private details.
- Use one to three examples to show style or format, and say what to copy.
- When results miss, add the missing context.

### Context that you set once: projects and custom instructions

Typing the same background into every chat gets tiring. Most assistants now let you store context:

- **Custom instructions or personalisation settings:** a short description of who you are and how you like answers ("I run a small bakery in Lahore; keep answers short; use British English").
- **Projects, Gems or custom assistants:** a workspace where you upload reference files (your price list, brand guide, FAQs) and write standing instructions. Every chat in that workspace can use them.
- **Memory:** some assistants can remember facts from earlier conversations, and let you view, edit or switch that memory off.

Feature names and availability change and differ between free and paid plans, so check your assistant's settings. We cover these in depth in module 4. The principle stays the same: the AI can only use context it can see.

### Hands-on: the context checklist

Before an important prompt, run through these five questions and add a line for each one that matters:

```text
1. Who am I?                 "I'm the office manager at a 12-person law firm."
2. What's the situation?     "Our printer lease ends next month."
3. What's the goal?          "Choose between renewing and buying."
4. What are the limits?      "Budget 2,000 GBP; must scan to email."
5. What material exists?     [paste the two quotes, with prices]
```

Then add one example if style or format matters.

### Worked example: examples that fix a tone problem

A UK charity asks for volunteer thank-you messages and keeps getting stiff, corporate text. Adding two real messages that volunteers loved fixes it instantly:

```text
Write 5 short thank-you messages for volunteers who helped at our food
bank this month. Match the warmth and length of these two real messages
(copy the style, not the content):

1. "Saturday wouldn't have happened without you. 212 families went home
   with full bags. Thank you, Priya."
2. "You turned up in the rain and still made everyone laugh. That's the
   spirit of this place. Thank you, Tom."

Volunteer names and what they did: [list]
```

### When examples backfire

Examples are powerful, so they can mislead. If both examples mention numbers, every output will include a number. If both are about food, the AI may drift toward food. Vary your examples and say what to copy: "Copy the length and warmth; the specific details should come from my list."

### How to know you gave enough context

Look at the answer for invented details: a made-up company name, a guessed price, a generic audience. Each invention marks a gap in your context. Fill the gap, and the invention disappears.

lessons.title: Iterating: the art of the follow-up
lessons.body:
### The first answer is a draft

Professionals rarely accept the first result. They treat it as a draft and steer. Iterating well is often faster than trying to write a perfect prompt up front.

### Five follow-up moves

**1. Adjust.** Change one thing at a time so you can see the effect.

```text
Good. Make it 30% shorter and replace the second paragraph with a
customer example.
```

**2. Point to specifics.** Quote the part you want changed.

```text
The line "we are passionate about quality" feels generic. Replace it
with something specific about our hand-stitched seams.
```

**3. Ask for options.** Instead of one version, ask for several and pick.

```text
Give me 3 alternative opening lines: one funny, one emotional, one direct.
```

**4. Explain what is wrong and why.** The AI learns your taste within the conversation.

```text
This sounds too salesy for our audience of nurses, who are sceptical of
marketing. Make it more practical and humble.
```

**5. Combine.** Take the best parts of different versions.

```text
Use the opening from version 2 and the ending from version 3.
```

### When to start fresh

Long conversations can drift. The AI may hold on to earlier instructions you have abandoned, or mix details from different drafts. Start a new chat when:

- you have changed direction significantly
- the answers are getting worse or repetitive
- the conversation has become very long

When you start fresh, write a new, better prompt that includes everything you learned: "Write X, for Y, in style Z, avoiding A and B." That improved prompt is now reusable.

### Ask the AI to critique itself

A simple, effective habit:

```text
Before I use this, review your draft against my requirements:
under 150 words, mentions the Friday deadline, friendly tone.
List anything that doesn't meet them, then fix it.
```

This catches missed requirements. It is not perfect, especially for facts, so you still need to check anything important yourself.

### Ask the AI to improve your prompt

You can also ask for help with the prompt itself:

```text
Here is a prompt I use to write weekly team updates. Suggest how to
make it clearer and more specific, then show me the improved version.
```

This is a great way to learn, because you see what the AI thinks is missing.

### Worked example: iterating an event invitation

A community organiser in Karachi drafts a volunteer invitation.

Round 1: "Write an invitation for volunteers for a beach clean-up on Saturday." Result: generic and long.

Round 2: "Make it under 80 words, suitable for WhatsApp, and add the time (7-10am), meeting point (Sea View, near the camel rides) and what to bring (water, hat, gloves provided)." Result: much better, but a bit formal.

Round 3: "Make it more energetic and friendly, with one emoji, and add a line asking people to reply 'IN' to confirm." Result: ready to send.

Round 4 (saving for later): "Now write me a reusable prompt I can use for future clean-up invitations, with blanks for date, time and location."

In four short messages, the organiser has a finished message *and* a template for next time.

### Save what works

Keep a simple document of prompts that worked well, with a note of what they are for. Over time you build a personal library, and your first attempts get better and better. Many AI tools also let you save custom instructions or reusable prompts; check your tool's settings.

### Common iteration mistakes

- Changing many things at once, so you cannot tell what helped.
- Saying "no, that's wrong" without saying what is wrong.
- Continuing a confused conversation instead of starting fresh with a better prompt.
- Forgetting to check facts after several rewrites, since errors can creep in.

### Hands-on: the three-message workout

Practise iteration deliberately with this routine on any real draft:

```text
Message 1 (the brief):
Write a 120-word LinkedIn post announcing that I passed my Google Ads
certification. Audience: small business owners in the UK who might hire
me. Tone: confident, not boastful.

Message 2 (point to specifics):
The opening "I'm thrilled to announce" is overused. Give me 3 alternative
first lines that start with a benefit for the reader.

Message 3 (combine and finish):
Use option 2 as the opening, keep the rest, and end with a question that
invites comments. Then list what you changed.
```

Asking the AI to list its changes makes it easy to review edits instead of re-reading everything.

### Editing in place

Many assistants now open longer drafts in a side panel or document view (for example a canvas or artifact-style editor) where you can highlight a sentence and ask for a change to just that part. Use it for long documents: targeted edits keep the parts you already like and avoid the whole text being rewritten each time.

### Branching instead of arguing

If an answer goes in the wrong direction, you do not need to argue with it for five messages. Most assistants let you **edit your earlier message** and regenerate, which creates a clean branch of the conversation. Fix the prompt at the point things went wrong rather than piling corrections on top.

### When iteration is not the answer

If you have sent four follow-ups and the answer is still not right, stop and diagnose. Usually one of three things is missing:

- **Information** the AI does not have (add context or paste material).
- **A clear picture of good** (add an example).
- **The right tool or mode** (for a hard calculation or multi-step plan, try a thinking mode; for current facts, turn on web search).

Then start a fresh chat with an improved prompt.

### How to measure your iteration skill

Keep a tally for a week: how many messages did it take to reach a usable result? Also note which follow-up moves worked best for you. Most people find that "point to specifics" and "explain why" do most of the work, and that their first prompts improve as they learn what they usually forget.

By the end, you will get usable results in fewer messages.

lessons.title: Formatting outputs: getting the shape you need
lessons.body:
### Format is part of the request

A great answer in the wrong shape still creates work. If you need a table for a spreadsheet, a bullet list for a slide, or plain text for WhatsApp, say so. AI assistants can produce almost any text format when asked clearly.

### Common formats and how to ask

**Bullet points:** "Summarise in 5 bullet points, each under 15 words."

**Numbered steps:** "Give me step-by-step instructions, numbered, one action per step."

**Tables:** "Put this in a table with columns: Product, Price, Main benefit, Best for."

**Email:** "Write it as an email with a subject line, greeting, 2 short paragraphs and sign-off."

**Headings:** "Organise the answer under three headings: Problem, Options, Recommendation."

**Plain text:** "Plain text only, no bullet points, bold text or headings; I'm pasting it into a text message."

**Spreadsheet-ready:** "Output as comma-separated values with a header row, so I can paste it into a spreadsheet."

**Checklist:** "Make it a checklist with tick boxes I can print."

### Length control

Be explicit and realistic:

- "One sentence."
- "Under 50 words."
- "About one page."
- "3 short paragraphs."

AI is better at counting items (bullets, paragraphs) than counting exact words, so use structure-based limits when precision matters.

### Tone and reading level

Tone is also format:

- "Friendly and casual, like a message to a colleague."
- "Formal, suitable for a government office."
- "Plain English; explain any technical term in brackets."
- "Suitable for a reading age of about 12."

### Language

You can ask for outputs in any major language, or in two at once:

```text
Write the announcement in English, then the same message in Urdu,
keeping the meaning identical.
```

For important translations, such as legal notices, medical instructions or contracts, have a fluent human check. AI translation can be very good but can miss nuance or local terms.

### Show the format with a template

If you need an exact structure, give a template for the AI to fill:

```text
Fill in this template for each of the 3 suppliers in my notes:

Supplier:
Price per unit:
Delivery time:
Strengths:
Concerns:
Recommendation (Yes/No/Maybe):
```

This is extremely reliable because there is little room for interpretation.

### Worked example: meeting notes to action table

A project coordinator pastes messy meeting notes and asks:

```text
From the notes below, create a table with columns:
Action | Owner | Deadline | Status.
If no deadline was mentioned, write "Not set".
Then, below the table, write a 2-sentence summary for people who
missed the meeting.

NOTES:
---
(paste notes)
---
```

Notice the instruction for missing information ("Not set"). Without it, the AI may invent a deadline to fill the column. Telling it what to do when information is missing is a simple habit that prevents made-up details.

### Formatting for where it will be used

Think about the destination:

- **Slides:** short bullets, no long sentences, one idea per bullet.
- **Social media:** platform length norms, line breaks, hashtags if appropriate.
- **Voice or video scripts:** written for speaking, short sentences, no bullet points or symbols.
- **Emails:** subject line, short paragraphs, clear request.
- **Documents:** headings, logical sections.

Tell the AI where the text will go: "This will be read aloud in a 30-second video."

### Common formatting mistakes

- Asking for a table but not naming the columns.
- Not saying what to do with missing information.
- Forgetting the destination, so text for a chat message arrives full of headings and bold.
- Expecting exact word counts; check and adjust.

### Quick practice

Try asking for the same information in two shapes, for example "a 5-bullet summary for my manager" and "a 3-sentence WhatsApp update for the team". Comparing them side by side trains your eye for which format suits which reader, and you will quickly start specifying format in your very first prompt instead of fixing it afterwards.

### Hands-on: one message, three destinations

Paste some real information (a price list, an event plan, your notes) and send this:

```text
Using the information below, produce three versions:

1. A table with columns: Item | Price | Notes. If a price is missing,
   write "TBC".
2. A WhatsApp message under 60 words, plain text, no bold or bullet
   symbols, with line breaks.
3. A 20-second voice-note script, written to be spoken, numbers written
   as words.

INFORMATION:
---
[paste here]
---
```

Compare the three. You are training yourself to name the destination in your first prompt.

### Getting data you can paste into a spreadsheet

For data you will analyse, ask for a format that pastes cleanly:

```text
Extract every order from the emails below into CSV with the header row:
date,customer,product,quantity,amount_gbp
Use ISO dates (YYYY-MM-DD). If a value is missing, leave it empty.
Output only the CSV, nothing before or after it.
```

"Output only the CSV" stops the assistant adding friendly sentences that break your paste. Many assistants can also create a downloadable spreadsheet or document file directly; if yours can, ask for "a downloadable .xlsx file" and check it opens correctly.

### Formatting in right-to-left and mixed languages

If you work in Arabic or Urdu, tell the assistant which language each part should be in and whether you need numerals in Western or Eastern Arabic style. Check the result in the app where it will be used, because right-to-left text can display differently in different apps.

### Tone presets you can reuse

Save three tone descriptions that match your real needs and paste them when required:

```text
TONE A (clients): warm, clear, professional; short sentences; no slang.
TONE B (social): friendly, energetic, one emoji maximum, a question at the end.
TONE C (internal): direct, bullet points, decisions and owners first.
```

### How to check format quickly

Before using an output, check the four things that most often go wrong: length, structure (are all the columns or sections there?), missing-information handling (did it invent anything to fill gaps?) and destination fit (does it look right where you will paste it?).

lessons.title: Quick answers, thinking modes and deep research
lessons.body:
### Three ways an assistant can answer

Modern assistants give you a choice of how much effort they put into an answer. The names differ between products and change often, but there are three broad modes:

| Mode | What it does | Typical wait | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quick answer** | Replies straight away from what it already knows and what you gave it | Seconds | Drafting, rewriting, summarising, simple questions |
| **Thinking (reasoning)** | Works through the problem privately before answering: breaks it down, tries approaches, checks its work | Seconds to minutes | Maths, multi-step plans, tricky decisions, logic, code |
| **Research (web search or deep research)** | Searches the web, reads many pages and writes a sourced report | Seconds for a search; several minutes for deep research | Current facts, comparisons, market scans, anything that needs sources |

Some assistants pick the mode automatically depending on your question; others give you a switch, a menu or a model picker labelled with words like "Thinking", "Reasoning", "Extended thinking", "Pro" or "Deep research". Check your assistant's interface and help pages, because these labels change frequently.

### Why thinking modes help on hard problems

A quick answer is like asking a colleague to reply on the spot. A thinking mode is like saying "take a few minutes and work it out properly". The model spends extra computation reasoning before it writes the answer. For problems with several steps, this usually reduces mistakes, because the model can catch and fix errors along the way.

It is not magic. Thinking modes still make mistakes, cost more on paid plans or use up usage limits faster, and are slower. On simple tasks they rarely add much.

### A decision guide

Ask yourself three questions:

1. **Does the answer depend on current information?** Prices, opening hours, laws, news, product specs. If yes, use web search or deep research, and check the sources.
2. **Does the task have several steps or constraints that must all be satisfied?** A schedule, a budget, a comparison with a recommendation, a calculation. If yes, use a thinking mode.
3. **Is it mainly about wording?** An email, a caption, a rewrite, a summary of text you pasted. Use the quick mode.

### Worked example: one business owner, three modes

Hina runs an online modest-fashion shop from Lahore that ships to the UAE and UK.

**Quick mode:** "Rewrite this product description to sound warmer, under 60 words." Done in seconds.

**Thinking mode:**

```text
I sell 3 abaya styles. Costs and prices are below. Shipping to the UAE
costs 18 USD per parcel and to the UK 22 USD. A parcel holds up to 3
items. Work out my profit per order for 1, 2 and 3 items to each
country, then tell me the minimum order value for free shipping that
keeps at least 25% margin. Show the calculation as a table and list any
assumptions.
[costs and prices]
```

The thinking mode is more likely to keep all the constraints straight. Hina still copies the table into a spreadsheet and checks the formulas.

**Deep research:**

```text
Research the current rules and typical costs for a small Pakistani
online seller shipping clothing to customers in the UAE and UK: customs
duty thresholds, VAT, and documentation needed. Use official government
and courier sources where possible, cite each claim, and flag anything
that changed in the last 12 months.
```

She then opens the official sources cited, because customs rules change and a report can misread them.

### How to prompt a thinking mode

Thinking modes need the same good briefing as any prompt, with three extra tips:

- **Give all the information up front.** The model can reason, but it cannot invent facts you did not supply.
- **Say what "done" looks like.** "A table with these columns and a one-line recommendation."
- **Don't micromanage the steps.** You do not need to write "think step by step"; the mode already does that. Describe the goal and constraints clearly instead.

### How to prompt deep research

Deep research tools plan a search, read many sources and produce a long report. Get more from them by stating:

- **The decision the research supports** ("so I can choose a courier").
- **Scope:** countries, time period, types of source to prefer or avoid.
- **Output:** length, sections, a comparison table, a list of sources.
- **What not to do:** "Don't include general advice; focus on rules and costs."

Many deep research tools ask clarifying questions before they start. Answer them properly; it is the best moment to shape the report.

### Hands-on: the same question in three modes

Pick one real question from your work that involves a few steps (a budget, a comparison or a plan). Ask it three ways:

```text
Quick mode:     [your question]
Thinking mode:  [same question] + "Check your answer against every
                constraint and list any assumptions."
Research mode:  [same question] + "Use current web sources and cite them."
```

Compare the three answers on accuracy, usefulness, time taken and how easy each was to check.

### Pitfalls

- Using thinking mode for everything and hitting usage limits by mid-week.
- Treating a long, confident research report as verified truth. Open the sources.
- Forgetting that a quick mode without web access may not know recent events.
- Assuming the "best" mode is always the newest or most expensive one.

### How to know you are choosing well

lessons.body:
### The problem: repeating yourself

If you use an assistant every day, you probably type the same background again and again: who you are, what your business does, your preferred tone. Modern assistants let you store that context so every conversation starts with it. This is the everyday version of what professionals call **context engineering**: deciding what information the AI sees before it answers.

### Three places to store context

**1. Custom instructions (or personalisation).** A short standing note that applies to all your chats. Typically two parts: what the assistant should know about you, and how you want it to respond.

**2. Projects (and similar workspaces).** Many assistants let you create a workspace with its own instructions and uploaded files. ChatGPT and Claude call these Projects; Gemini offers Gems; Microsoft Copilot has notebooks and agents in some plans. Names and features vary by plan and change often, so check your own assistant. Everything in the workspace (your brand guide, price list, FAQs) is available to every chat inside it.

**3. Memory.** Some assistants remember useful facts from past chats. You can usually see, edit and delete memories, or switch the feature off.

### Writing good custom instructions

Keep them short, factual and stable. Things that change weekly belong in the prompt, not here.

```text
About me:
I run a 4-person digital marketing agency in Manchester. Clients are
local restaurants, gyms and salons. I write in British English.

How to respond:
- Be concise: lead with the answer, then detail if needed.
- Use prices in GBP and UK examples unless I say otherwise.
- When you are unsure of a fact, say so rather than guessing.
- For anything I will publish, flag claims I should verify.
```

Avoid vague lines like "be amazing" or long lists of rules. Each line should change the answer in a way you want.

### Setting up a project that works

A good project has three parts:

1. **A clear purpose:** one client, one product line, one recurring job (for example "Weekly social posts for Bloom Café").
2. **Standing instructions:** the brief that applies to every chat in the project.
3. **Reference files:** the few documents the AI really needs.

Example project instructions:

```text
Purpose: draft social posts and replies for Bloom Café, a family café
in Abu Dhabi.

Always:
- Use the brand voice guide (file: bloom-voice.pdf): warm, playful,
  never sarcastic.
- Use prices from the current menu (file: menu-sept-2026.pdf) only.
- Write in English; add an Arabic version when I ask.
- Keep captions under 80 words with at most 2 emojis.

Never:
- Invent offers, prices or opening hours. If something is not in the
  files, ask me.
- Mention competitors.
```

### Choosing the right files

More files are not always better. The assistant has to decide what is relevant, and outdated files cause confident mistakes. Keep files:

- **Current:** delete last season's menu when the new one arrives.
- **Focused:** the brand guide and the menu, not every document you own.
- **Clearly named:** "menu-sept-2026.pdf" is better than "final_v3.pdf".

### Memory: helpful and risky

Memory saves time, but it can also surprise you. An assistant might remember that you once asked for a formal tone and apply it everywhere. Review memories regularly, delete anything wrong or outdated, and switch memory off for sensitive topics. Never rely on memory for anything critical; put important facts in the prompt or project files.

### Worked example: an agency with many clients

Omar runs a small agency in Riyadh with six clients. He used to paste each client's details into every chat and still got mixed-up tones. Now he has one project per client, each with the brand guide, product list and standing instructions. His custom instructions hold only his own preferences. Results are more consistent, and when a new team member joins, the projects double as onboarding documentation.

### Privacy and workplace rules

Anything you put in custom instructions, projects or memory is stored by the provider. Before uploading client documents:

- Check your organisation's AI policy and which plan it approves (business and enterprise plans typically offer stronger data controls).
- Remove personal data you do not need, such as customer phone numbers and addresses.
- Check whether your plan uses your content for model training and how to opt out if appropriate.

### Hands-on: set up your first project in 15 minutes

1. Choose one recurring task (weekly newsletter, client replies, lesson plans).
2. Create a project or workspace in your assistant (or, if yours has none, a saved text you paste at the start of each chat).
3. Write standing instructions using the Purpose, Always, Never structure above.
4. Upload one or two current reference files.
5. Test with three real tasks. Note anything the assistant got wrong and add a line to the instructions to fix it.

### How to know it is working

Your prompts get shorter while the results get more consistent. If you still have to repeat a detail in most chats, add it to the instructions. If answers include outdated facts, clean up your files or memory.

### Assistants can see, read and listen

Most major assistants now accept more than typed text. You can upload PDFs, spreadsheets and slides; take a photo with your phone; share a screenshot; or simply talk. The same prompting principles apply: say what the material is, what you want done with it, and what good output looks like.

### Files: PDFs, documents and spreadsheets

When you upload a file, the assistant reads its text and, in many products, looks at page images too, which helps with tables and charts. Good habits:

- **Say what the file is and why you uploaded it.** "This is our 2026 staff handbook. I need to answer employee questions about annual leave."
- **Ask for page or section references** so you can check answers.
- **Narrow the job:** "Using only section 4" is more reliable than "Summarise everything".
- **For spreadsheets,** ask the assistant to calculate using its analysis tools rather than estimate, and check a few numbers yourself.

```text
Attached is our supplier contract (PDF, 18 pages). I need to know:
1. The notice period to end the contract.
2. Any penalties for late payment.
3. Whether prices can change during the contract.
For each, quote the exact clause and give the page number. If the
contract doesn't say, write "Not stated". Keep the answer under 200 words.
```

### Photos and screenshots

A phone photo or screenshot can save a lot of typing:

- **Receipts and invoices:** "Extract the date, supplier, total and currency into a table. Write UNREADABLE for anything you can't read clearly."
- **Error messages:** "This is a screenshot of an error in our booking software. What does it mean and what should I try first?"
- **Whiteboards and handwritten notes:** "Turn this whiteboard photo into a tidy action list with owners."
- **Products and places:** "What kind of plant is this and how often should I water it indoors in Dubai's climate?"
- **Design feedback:** "Here are two versions of our flyer. Which is easier to read from two metres away, and why?"

Tips: crop to what matters, take photos flat and in good light, and label multiple images ("Image 1 is the old menu, image 2 the new one"). Before sharing, blur or crop out anything private: faces of people who have not agreed, names, addresses, card numbers.

### Voice mode

Voice mode lets you talk to the assistant and hear its reply. It is excellent for:

- practising interviews, presentations or a new language;
- brainstorming while walking or driving (hands-free and safely);
- getting quick explanations when typing is awkward.

Prompting by voice works best when you set the scene first: "I'm going to practise a sales call. You play a busy restaurant owner who is sceptical about social media ads. Keep your replies short. After five minutes, give me feedback." Some assistants can also look through your phone camera during a voice conversation and talk about what they see; check the feature and its privacy settings before using it with other people around.

### Worked example: a clinic manager in Karachi

A clinic manager photographs a handwritten weekly rota, uploads the staff leave policy PDF, and asks:

```text
Image: this week's handwritten staff rota.
File: our leave policy.
1. Type the rota into a table (Day | Morning | Evening). Mark anything
   unreadable as "?".
2. Check it against the policy: flag anyone scheduled on approved leave
   days or working more than 5 shifts.
Quote the policy rule for each issue.
```

The assistant produces the table and flags two issues. The manager confirms the two "?" entries with the staff directly and corrects one misread name. Total time: ten minutes instead of forty.

### What assistants still get wrong

- **Blurry or tiny text** may be misread or even invented. Ask for UNREADABLE instead of guesses.
- **Long documents:** details in the middle can be missed. Ask for page references and check.
- **Charts:** assistants describe trends well but can misread exact values. Use the underlying data when you have it.
- **Counting** many small objects in a photo is unreliable.

### Hands-on: three multimodal tasks

Try one task of each type this week:

```text
1. FILE: upload a policy, contract or report and ask three questions,
   requiring a quote and page number for each answer.
2. PHOTO: photograph a receipt or handwritten note and ask for a table,
   with UNREADABLE for anything unclear.
3. VOICE: use voice mode to practise a 3-minute conversation you have
   coming up, then ask for feedback on clarity and confidence.
```

### How to know you are doing it well

For files and photos: every important answer can be traced to a page or part of the image, and you checked it. For voice: you finish the session with specific feedback you can act on, not just a pleasant chat.

lessons.body:
### Describing pictures, not intentions

Many assistants can now create images from a description, and some can generate short videos. Image models respond to **visual description**. "Make a picture that increases sales" gives them nothing to draw. "A bright flat-lay photo of a glass of mango lassi on a white marble table, fresh mango slices beside it, soft morning light, lots of empty space on the right for text" does.

### The five-part image prompt

1. **Subject:** what is in the picture, with specifics (colours, materials, number of items).
2. **Setting:** where it is and what is around it.
3. **Style:** photo, illustration, watercolour, 3D render, flat icon, vintage poster.
4. **Light and mood:** soft daylight, golden hour, studio lighting, cosy, energetic.
5. **Layout and format:** close-up or wide, where the subject sits, space for text, and the shape (square for a feed post, tall for a story, wide for a banner).

```text
A cosy illustration of a small bookshop at night in a rainy London
street, warm yellow light glowing from the window, a cat asleep on a
stack of books in the window display. Style: soft watercolour with ink
outlines. Wide format, with empty sky at the top for a headline.
```

### Editing by conversation

The newest image tools let you refine an image by talking to it: "Make the cat ginger", "Move the text space to the left", "Same scene but in daylight". You can also upload a reference image, for example your own product photo, and ask for a new background. Change one thing at a time so you can see what each instruction does.

### Text inside images

Image models have become much better at writing text inside images, but mistakes still happen, especially with long phrases, small fonts or non-Latin scripts. For anything you will publish (prices, dates, Arabic or Urdu headlines), add the text afterwards in a design tool such as Canva, or check every letter carefully.

### Short videos

Video generators create short clips from a description or from a starting image. The same principles apply, plus two extras:

- **One clear action per shot:** "steam rises from a cup as a hand places a pastry beside it."
- **Camera words:** close-up, wide shot, slow push-in, slow pan, static camera.

```text
Close-up of a hand pouring chai from a steel kettle into a glass cup on
a wooden table, steam rising, early morning light through a window.
Slow push-in, calm and warm, realistic.
```

Longer stories are built by generating several short shots and editing them together. Video generation is slower and often costs more than images, so plan the shot before you generate.

### Rules you must follow

- **People and likeness:** never create realistic images or videos of real people without their consent, and never to mislead.
- **Honest marketing:** if you show a product, it must look like what customers will receive. Advertising rules in the UK, US, UAE, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan all prohibit misleading ads. Use real product photos for the product itself.
- **Labels and disclosure:** many platforms require or offer labels for realistic AI-generated content. Follow each platform's rules.
- **Copyright:** avoid asking for copyrighted characters or a named living artist's style. Check the tool's terms for commercial use.
- **Representation:** default images can reflect stereotypes. Describe people deliberately and review results.

### Worked example: a café launch post

A café in Islamabad launches a new saffron cake.

1. They photograph the real cake.
2. They ask an image tool: "Place this cake on a rustic wooden table with soft window light and dried rose petals around it; keep the cake exactly as it is." They check the cake has not been changed.
3. They generate three versions, pick one, and add the headline and price in Canva.
4. They post with the platform's AI label where required.

### Hands-on: your first three images

```text
1. Write a five-part prompt (subject, setting, style, light, layout) for
   an image you actually need.
2. Generate it, then make exactly two conversational edits, one change
   each time.
3. Write a second prompt for the same idea in a completely different
   style and compare which suits your audience better.
```

### How to judge an image

Score each result from 1 to 3 on four questions: Does it match the prompt? Does it fit the brand? Are there visual errors (hands, text, odd objects)? Is it honest about the product? Only publish images that score well on all four.

lessons.title: Research with web search, deep research and sources
lessons.body:
### From "the AI said" to "the source says"

Ordinary chat answers come from what the model learned during training, which can be out of date or simply wrong. When an assistant **searches the web**, it reads current pages and cites them. When it runs **deep research**, it plans a series of searches, reads many sources and writes a long, structured report with citations. Assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity all offer versions of these features, with different names and limits by plan.

Search and citations change your job: instead of trusting the answer, you check the sources behind it.

### When to use which

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| A quick current fact (opening hours, a product spec, today's exchange rate) | Web search |
| A comparison or overview across many sources (suppliers, tools, regulations) | Deep research |
| Explaining a concept that does not change (what is a profit margin?) | Normal chat |
| Your own documents | Upload the file instead of searching |

### Writing a strong research prompt

A research prompt needs more direction than a chat prompt, because the assistant will make many choices on your behalf.

```text
GOAL: I'm choosing an email marketing tool for a small online shop in
the UK with 3,000 subscribers.

QUESTION: Compare 4 widely used email marketing tools on: monthly price
for 3,000 contacts, ease of use for non-technical users, e-commerce
integrations (Shopify), automation features, and UK/EU data handling.

SOURCES: Prefer the vendors' official pricing and documentation pages
and recent independent reviews. Ignore affiliate listicles.

OUTPUT: A comparison table, then a 150-word recommendation for my
situation, then a list of sources with dates. Flag any price you could
not confirm on an official page.
```

The parts that matter most: the **decision** the research supports, the **criteria**, the **type of sources**, and what to do with **uncertainty**.

### Checking a research report

Deep research reports look authoritative. They are long, well formatted and full of links. That makes them easy to over-trust. Use this routine:

1. **Spot-check the key claims.** Open the sources behind the three claims your decision depends on most.
2. **Check dates.** Prices, rules and product features change. Is each source recent enough?
3. **Look for missing viewpoints.** Did it only read vendor pages? Did it skip an important option?
4. **Watch for citation mismatch.** Sometimes a link is real but does not support the sentence it is attached to.
5. **Ask for the gaps:** "What could not be confirmed? Where did sources disagree?"

### Worked example: a founder in Dubai

Sara is setting up a small online skincare business in Dubai and asks a deep research tool about labelling and registration requirements for cosmetics. The report is clear and cites several pages. She opens them and finds that two citations are to a general blog, while the official municipality and federal authority pages give more specific requirements. She re-runs the research asking it to "use only official UAE government and regulator sources, and list each requirement with the authority responsible". The second report is shorter but far more useful. She still confirms the final checklist with the relevant authority before launching.

### Search for local and multilingual questions

If your question is about a specific country or city, say so. Search results differ by location and language. For markets like Pakistan, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, ask the assistant to also search in Urdu or Arabic where relevant, and to prefer official government sources.

### Hands-on: a mini research sprint

```text
1. Choose a real decision you face (a tool, a supplier, a rule you must
   follow).
2. Write a research prompt with GOAL, QUESTION, SOURCES and OUTPUT.
3. Run it with web search or deep research.
4. Open the sources for the three most important claims. Mark each as
   Confirmed, Partly confirmed or Not supported.
5. Send one follow-up asking the assistant to fix anything you could
   not confirm.
```

### Pitfalls

- Treating the number of citations as a sign of quality.
- Asking open-ended questions ("tell me about marketing") that produce long, generic reports.
- Using research for private or internal questions that the web cannot answer.
- Forgetting that research tools can take several minutes and may count against usage limits.

### How to know your research prompt worked

You end with a decision or a short list, every key claim is backed by a source you opened, and the report told you clearly what it could not confirm.

lessons.title: Patterns for writing and editing (1-18)
lessons.body:
### How to use this library

Each pattern below is a reusable shape. Replace the parts in square brackets with your details. Mix and match: most real prompts combine two or three patterns. Always add the basics from earlier modules (audience, format, length) when they matter.

### Drafting patterns

**1. The briefed draft**

```text
Write a [type of text] for [audience] about [topic]. The goal is [goal].
Length: [length]. Tone: [tone].
```

**2. The style match**

```text
Here is something I wrote that I like: "[sample]". Write a [new piece]
about [topic] in the same style. Copy the style, not the content.
```

**3. The outline first**

```text
Before writing, give me an outline for a [piece] about [topic] with
3-5 sections. Wait for my approval before writing the full text.
```

**4. The fill-the-template**

```text
Write a [piece] using this structure: [section 1], [section 2], [section 3].
```

**5. The multi-version**

```text
Write 3 versions of [text]: one [style A], one [style B], one [style C].
```

**6. The interview-me**

```text
I need to write [piece]. Ask me up to 5 questions first, then write it
using my answers.
```

### Editing patterns

**7. The tone shift**

```text
Rewrite this to sound more [warm / formal / confident / playful],
keeping the meaning the same: "[text]"
```

**8. The shorten**

```text
Cut this to under [N] words without losing [the key point / the deadline]: "[text]"
```

**9. The simplify**

```text
Rewrite this so a [12-year-old / non-expert / busy executive] can
understand it: "[text]"
```

**10. The proofread with reasons**

```text
Proofread this. List each change you made and why, then give the
corrected version: "[text]"
```

**11. The keep-my-voice edit**

```text
Improve the clarity and flow of this, but keep my voice and word
choices where possible. Only change what's needed: "[text]"
```

**12. The strengthen the opening**

```text
Give me 5 stronger first sentences for this piece: "[text]"
```

**13. The critic**

```text
Act as a demanding editor. Give me the 3 biggest weaknesses in this
draft and how to fix each. Don't rewrite it yet: "[text]"
```

### Specific-format patterns

**14. The email reply**

```text
Draft a reply to this email. I want to [accept / decline / ask for X].
Keep it [length], [tone]. Email: "[paste]"
```

**15. The social caption**

```text
Write a [platform] caption for [what the post shows]. Audience:
[audience]. Include [a call to action / 3 hashtags]. Under [N] words.
```

**16. The headline set**

```text
Write 10 headlines for [article] aimed at [audience]. Mix curiosity,
benefit-led and number-led styles.
```

**17. The translation with nuance**

```text
Translate this into [language] for [audience in country]. Keep the tone
[tone] and adapt any expressions that won't make sense locally: "[text]"
```

**18. The script**

```text
Turn this into a [30-second / 2-minute] spoken script for [video / voice note].
Short sentences, no bullet points: "[text]"
```

### Worked example: combining patterns

A freelance designer in Riyadh needs to send a price increase notice to clients. She combines the interview-me (6), briefed draft (1) and critic (13) patterns:

1. "I need to tell my clients my rates are going up 15% from next quarter. Ask me up to 5 questions first."
2. She answers: loyal clients, rates unchanged for 3 years, new services added, wants to keep relationships warm.
3. The AI drafts a warm, confident email.
4. "Act as a demanding editor. What are the 3 biggest weaknesses?" The AI notes the email apologises too much and buries the date.
5. "Fix those three issues."

Five short messages produce a better email than an hour of staring at a blank page.

### Tips for writing patterns

- Always give the AI your real material to work with: a draft, notes, facts. It will invent details otherwise.
- For anything public, check names, numbers and claims before publishing.
- When your brand or industry has rules (for example advertising disclosure rules for sponsored posts, or financial promotion rules), say so in the prompt and still check the output yourself.
- Save your best combinations as personal templates.

### Your turn

Choose three patterns you have never used and try each on a real task this week. Note which ones save you the most time.

### Hands-on: build your own pattern card

A pattern becomes yours when you adapt it to your real work. Take one pattern from this lesson and turn it into a card you can reuse:

```text
PATTERN CARD
Name: Client update email (from pattern 1 + 11)
When to use: every Friday for active clients
Prompt:
  Write a weekly update email to [client name] about [project].
  What we did this week: [bullets]
  What's next: [bullets]
  Anything we need from them: [bullets or "nothing"]
  Tone: warm, confident, concise. Under 150 words. Keep my phrasing
  where possible.
What to check: dates, names, promises about deadlines.
```

Store cards in a note or document, or inside your assistant's saved prompts or project instructions if it supports them.

### Patterns and thinking modes

Most writing patterns work best in the assistant's normal, fast mode. Thinking modes help with writing tasks that involve planning or logic, such as structuring a long report, reconciling conflicting feedback, or checking that a policy document is consistent. For a caption or an email, the fast mode is usually faster and just as good.

### Disclosure and honesty in AI-assisted writing

When you publish AI-assisted writing, the usual rules still apply. Sponsored or affiliate content needs a clear disclosure such as "#ad" or "Paid partnership" under advertising rules in many countries (for example the ASA and CAP Code in the UK and FTC guidance in the US). Reviews and testimonials must be genuine. Some workplaces, schools and publications require you to say when AI helped. When in doubt, check the rules and be open.

### Measuring whether a pattern earns its place

Track two things for each pattern you use regularly: minutes saved compared with writing from scratch, and how much editing the output needs. Keep the patterns that save time with light edits; rework or drop the rest.

lessons.body:
### Analysis patterns

Analysis is where AI can save hours, as long as you give it the material and check its conclusions.

**19. The summary for a reader**

```text
Summarise this for [reader] who has [2 minutes / no background].
Focus on [what matters to them]: "[text]"
```

**20. The key points and gaps**

```text
List the key points in this document, then list any important
questions it doesn't answer: "[text]"
```

**21. The compare**

```text
Compare [option A] and [option B] for [my situation] in a table:
cost, effort, risks, benefits, best for.
```

**22. The pros and cons with weight**

```text
List the pros and cons of [decision] for [who]. Mark each as
high, medium or low importance and explain briefly.
```

**23. The theme finder**

```text
Here are [customer comments / survey answers]. Group them into themes,
count how many comments fit each theme, and give one example quote each.
```

**24. The explain the numbers**

```text
Here is a small table of [data]. Describe the main patterns in plain
language, and tell me what you can't conclude from this data alone.
```

**25. The devil's advocate**

```text
Here is my plan: [plan]. Argue against it as strongly as you can.
What would a sceptic say?
```

**26. The assumption check**

```text
What assumptions am I making in this plan? Which ones are riskiest
if they're wrong? [plan]
```

**27. The extract**

```text
From the text below, extract every [date / name / price / action]
into a list. If something is unclear, mark it "unclear": "[text]"
```

**28. The decision helper**

```text
I'm deciding between [options]. My priorities, in order, are [1, 2, 3].
Ask me any questions you need, then recommend one and explain why.
```

### Brainstorming patterns

Brainstorming is where AI's speed shines. Quantity first, then filter.

**29. The big list**

```text
Give me 20 ideas for [goal] for [audience]. One line each. Include
some unusual ones.
```

**30. The constraint twist**

```text
Give me 10 ideas for [goal] that cost less than [budget] and can be done
in [time].
```

**31. The perspective shift**

```text
How would [a teenager / a busy parent / a retiree / a competitor] see
[product or idea]? Give 3 ideas from each perspective.
```

**32. The combine**

```text
Combine ideas from [field A] and [field B] to generate 10 new ideas for [goal].
```

**33. The name generator**

```text
Suggest 15 names for [product / event / business]. Criteria: [short,
easy to spell, works in English and Arabic]. Explain the idea behind each.
```

**34. The build on mine**

```text
Here are my 3 ideas: [ideas]. Build on each with 3 variations, then
suggest 3 new ones in a different direction.
```

**35. The filter and rank**

```text
From the ideas above, pick the best 5 for [criteria] and rank them,
with one sentence each on why.
```

**36. The what could go wrong**

```text
For my idea [idea], list the 5 most likely ways it could fail and how
to prevent each.
```

**37. The first step**

```text
For the top idea, what is the smallest, cheapest test I could run
this week to see if it works?
```

### Worked example: from comments to action

A café owner in Manchester pastes 40 online reviews and uses patterns 23, 26 and 29:

1. Theme finder: themes include slow weekend service, loved pastries, limited seating, and friendly staff.
2. She checks the counts against a few reviews herself (the AI's counts can be off, so spot-check).
3. Assumption check on her plan to extend opening hours: "You're assuming the complaints about seating are from people who would come at later hours."
4. Big list: 20 ideas to reduce weekend waits; she picks a pre-order option and a second till.

### Important cautions for analysis

- **Give it the data.** Without your real material, the AI will produce generic analysis that sounds specific.
- **Check counts and numbers.** AI can miscount or miscalculate, especially with long lists. Spot-check, or use a spreadsheet for exact numbers.
- **Correlation is not cause.** If the AI says "sales rose because of the campaign", ask what else could explain it.
- **You own the decision.** Use AI to widen your thinking, not to replace your judgement.

### Hands-on: a mini analysis you can finish in 15 minutes

Paste 15 to 30 real comments (reviews, survey answers or feedback, with names and contact details removed) and run this three-step sequence:

```text
Step 1: Group these comments into 4-6 themes. For each theme give a
count, a one-line description and one short example quote. Put any
comment that fits no theme under "Other".

Step 2: Which theme would most improve customer satisfaction if fixed?
Give your reasoning and say what you can't tell from this data alone.

Step 3: Give me 10 low-cost ideas to fix that theme, then rank the top 3
by effort and likely impact.
```

Then do the human part: pick three comments at random and check they were placed in a sensible theme, and recount one theme yourself.

### When to switch on a thinking mode

For analysis, a thinking or reasoning mode is often worth the extra wait when:

- the question has several steps ("compare three suppliers across price, delivery and risk, then recommend one");
- numbers must be combined ("work out the break-even point");
- you want the assistant to challenge a plan properly (devil's advocate, assumption check).

For quick theme-finding or simple summaries, the normal mode is usually enough. If your assistant can run code or analyse uploaded spreadsheets, ask it to calculate rather than estimate, and check that it did.

### Brainstorming with better spread

AI brainstorms can feel samey. Three fixes:

```text
- "Give me ideas in 4 different categories: cheap, bold, digital, community."
- "Include 3 ideas that most businesses in my industry would dismiss."
- "Don't include anything that needs a budget above 500 GBP."
```

### Measuring an analysis prompt

A good analysis prompt produces conclusions you can trace back to the data. If you cannot find the comments behind a theme, or the counts are clearly wrong, the analysis is not usable yet. Ask for quotes and counts every time; they make checking fast.
